power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .481", "p = .691", "p = .303", "p = .418" ), Sentence = c("The baseline model was not statistically significant F(3, 111) = 0.83, p = .481, and did not account for significant variance in boredom proneness, R² = .02, adjusted R² = -.01.", "None of the individual predictors reached significance (age: β = -.04, p = .691; sex: β = -.10, p = .303; cardiac interoceptive accuracy: β = -.08, p = .418).", "None of the individual predictors reached significance (age: β = -.04, p = .691; sex: β = -.10, p = .303; cardiac interoceptive accuracy: β = -.08, p = .418).", "None of the individual predictors reached significance (age: β = -.04, p = .691; sex: β = -.10, p = .303; cardiac interoceptive accuracy: β = -.08, p = .418)." )), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. text.text: Boredom proneness has been linked to a disrupted relationship with one's internal states, yet the mechanism underlying this disruption remains unclear.
One possibility is that this disruption reflects a difficulty in translating interoceptive signals into meaningful predictions about internal states, rather than a basic failure to detect them.
Across two studies, we examined whether this disrupted relationship reflects interpretive challenges, a deficit in cardiac interoceptive accuracy, or both.

Study 1 (N = 124) was a direct replication confirming that highly boredom prone individuals report attending intensely to bodily sensations while struggling to interpret them -a pattern that held across a combined sample of 350 adults and yielded moderate-to-strong correlations with established measures of self-focused attention and interoceptive sensory confusion.
Study 2 (N = 121) administered a heartbeat counting task to determine whether this disrupted relationship was due to deficient interoceptive processing or interpretive failure.
Boredom proneness was unrelated to objective heartbeat counting accuracy but remained associated with self-reported interoceptive sensory confusion.
Converging with Study 1, this pattern suggests that boredom proneness is best characterized by a difficulty in interpreting internal signals than by a basic interoceptive perceptual deficit.
Together, these findings are consistent with predictive processing accounts of boredom proneness where those high in trait boredom struggle to generate meaningful predictions from interoceptive cues.

Whether this dissociation between self-reported and objective cardiac interoception generalizes across different measurement approaches and populations remains an open question that future work could examine using more sensitive interoceptive tasks and trial-level prediction error metrics.
Boredom is a negatively valenced experience born of the feeling of wanting but failing to engage successfully with the world (Goldberg et al., 2011; Van Tilburg & Igou, 2011).

text.text: Understanding interoceptive signals may therefore be essential for maintaining both affective (Barrett et al., 2016) and cognitive (Trudel et al., 2025) homeostasis by informing self-regulatory processes and accurately predicting the outcomes of intended actions.

text.text: Thus, a chronic failure to decode these inner cues may be a key contributor to trait boredom proneness.
We report data from two studies that build on these previous findings.

Study 1 is a direct replication of Trudel and colleagues (2024), examining the association between boredom proneness and two facets of interoceptive processing: heightened self-focused awareness and interoceptive sensory confusion.

text.text: Replicating this pattern would strengthen the notion that boredom prone individuals are acutely oriented toward their own internal states yet struggle to make sense of them.
Study 2 examines the hypothesis that misinterpreting interoceptive cues may contribute to trait boredom proneness.
There are two possible explanations for the interoceptive dysfunction reported by individuals prone to boredom.
First, boredom proneness could stem from a deficit in interoceptive accuracy (i.e., an impaired ability to accurately perceive internal bodily signals).
Such a deficit would make it difficult for these individuals to assign meaning to their affective states.
Second, boredom proneness may result from a challenge in interpreting interoceptive signals rather than a failure to accurately represent such signals.
In this case, internal signals may be accurately detected but poorly translated into coherent emotional states.
To adjudicate between these accounts, we administered a heartbeat counting task as an index of objective cardiac interoceptive accuracy (Schandry, 1981).

text.text: If boredom proneness reflects a detection deficit, accuracy on the heartbeat task should decrease as boredom proneness increases.
If instead, boredom proneness reflects an interpretive failure, it should be associated with greater interoceptive sensory confusion independent of heartbeat detection accuracy.

text.text: The results of Study 1 replicated prior work and supported the hypothesis that people who are highly prone to boredom tend to focus intently on their internal bodily sensations but struggle to make sense of them.

When combined (i.e., data from Trudel et al., 2024 and the two samples tested here), the pooled adult sample (N = 471) yields moderate-to-strong positive correlations between trait boredom and an excessive focus on internal states coupled with the struggle to interpret those very states.

text.text: This inconsistency may suggest that these measures do not function as reliable indices of a single underlying construct but rather capture different facets of interoceptive processing.

However, the Self-Awareness Questionnaire (SAQ) and Interoceptive Sensory Questionnaire (ISQ) target precisely the two components of our central argument: that boredom prone individuals struggle at the interpretive stage of interoception despite attending well, or perhaps excessively, to their bodily experiences.
The SAQ taps into the sensing side with higher scores indicating a heightened, recurring tendency to direct attention inward.
This is consistent with earlier research showing that elevated self-focus does not necessarily correspond to improved self-knowledge (Bambrah et al., 2023).
text.formatted: This is consistent with earlier research showing that elevated self-focus does not necessarily correspond to improved self-knowledge <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bambrah et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, the ISQ addresses the lack of clarity, reflecting a particular challenge in making sense of inner experiences, with participants reporting confusion or overlap in their interpretation of bodily sensations.

If boredom proneness is characterized by increased internal focus and confused interpretation rather than a general interoceptive perceptual deficit, then only measures capturing these specific features should consistently correlate with trait boredom across samples as they did here (see Tables 1 and 2 and Supplementary Material S1).

text.text: Results from Study 2 did not find evidence that boredom proneness was associated with reduced accuracy in perceiving interoceptive signals, at least in the domain of heartbeat counting.

Although highly boredom prone individuals reported struggling to make sense of their interoceptive cues despite attending to them -relations evident across three separate samples now -objective heartbeat estimates did not vary significantly as a function of boredom proneness.
These results suggest that boredom proneness may be more closely tied to how individuals attend to and interpret internal signals, rather than detection fidelity.

In Trudel and colleagues (2024) study, interoceptive sensory confusion (ISQ) and selfawareness (SAQ) together explained an additional 5% of variance in boredom proneness after controlling for other factors known to correlate with the trait (i.e., alexithymia, self-control, and body awareness).

Here, we chose a more conservative covariate set (age, sex, and cardiac interoceptive accuracy) as a neutral baseline model to provide a direct test of our hypothesis and observed a substantially larger increment (ΔR² = .23).

Notably, cardiac interoceptive accuracy did not predict boredom proneness, indicating that the observed increment was specifically driven by self-reported interoceptive measures rather than objective performance.

The dissociation between objective (i.e., heartbeat counting accuracy) and self-report measures of interoception aligns with a growing body of evidence suggesting these dimensions are only weakly related and may reflect distinct physiological and metacognitive processes (Forkmann et al., 2016; Garfinkel et al., 2015).

text.text: In addition, the heartbeat counting task used here may lack the sensitivity to detect differences that are well captured by self-report.

Given that boredom may slow the experience of time (Wolff et al., 2025) and that highly boredom prone individuals tend to overestimate durations (Danckert & Allman, 2005), we would expect such strategy to produce either an overestimation or, at least, less underestimation of heart rate as a function of boredom proneness.

text.text: Together, these findings suggest that cardiac interoceptive measures index at least partly distinct abilities, raising the possibility that the present null findings are specific to the heartbeat counting task rather than to cardiac interoception more broadly.
One further constraint of these findings relates to the organ-specific nature of interoceptive processes.

Although Herbert and colleagues (2012) linked cardiac awareness to gastric sensitivity, Garfinkel and colleagues (2016) reported a dissociation between cardiac and respiratory accuracy alongside a positive relationship between their awareness metrics.

text.text: This suggests that task performance is domain-specific while metacognitive insight may generalize across domains.
Banellis and colleagues (2026) recently extended this pattern in a large-scale psychophysical study (N = 241).
They reported a modest positive correlation for self-reported confidence but no crossmodality correlation for sensitivity, precision or metacognitive accuracy between cardiac and respiratory tasks.
These findings raise the possibility that subjective interoceptive sensory confusion, assuming it behaves similarly to confidence and awareness measures, may be more domain general.
In contrast, objective interoceptive accuracy may be task specific.

Whether the dissociation between self-reported and objective cardiac interoception observed here in relation to trait boredom proneness holds across other interoceptive domains remains to be tested directly.

text.text: In other words, trait boredom proneness may stem from differences in how the brain integrates interoceptive signals to represent emotions such as boredom in order to predict the best way to alleviate the discomfort, rather than from differences in how those interoceptive cues are perceived per se.
Lastly, other compensatory mechanisms may be at play to offset the perceived struggle highly boredom prone individuals have in making sense of interoceptive cues.

An alternative explanation of these results could be linked to previous research suggesting that cardiac interoceptive accuracy plays a role primarily in how intensely emotions are experienced (Wiens et al., 2000).

text.text: That is, good heartbeat detectors reported feeling emotions more intensely.

While the causal direction of this relationship remains unclear, feeling boredom more intensely than most (a cardinal sign of boredom proneness) coupled with heightened self-awareness, may boost heartbeat counting performance for individuals experiencing chronic boredom, even when they report interoceptive sensory confusion.

Perhaps these features of chronic boredom -elevated emotional intensity and heightened self-focus -are sufficient to obscure group differences in objective interoceptive accuracy as measured here on the heartbeat counting task.
Future versions of the task could incorporate trial-by-trial confidence ratings, in which participants predict their own accuracy.

The discrepancy between predicted and actual accuracy would yield an interoceptive prediction error score -a metric that could more directly index the interpretive failures implicated in boredom proneness (see Garfinkel et al., 2015 for an example of this approach).

text.text: Building on this, further research could investigate whether highly boredom prone individuals differ from their low boredom prone counterparts in other aspects of how they generate and update predictions about their own interoceptive performance.
More broadly, high boredom proneness may involve a general failure to reconcile prediction errors by updating engagement expectations based on feedback.
Alternatively, it may reflect a narrower range of predictions, where the highly boredom prone report similarly confident estimates despite performance fluctuations.

Either pattern would extend the predictive processing account introduced earlier to the specific case of interoceptive performance monitoring, indicating a failure to generate or update accurate predictions about one's own bodily signals rather than the external world.

Since self-regulation relies on interoceptive signals to anticipate which activities will resolve an unsatisfying state, an interpretive failure-rather than a failure to detect those signals-may explain the inability of the highly boredom prone to translate bodily cues into effective exploratory actions.
